name: Quantisation for Inference (FP8, INT4, KV Cache)
question: Can a big model run on fewer GPUs without losing quality?
summary: Quantisation stores a model’s weights, and sometimes its activations and KV cache, in fewer bits so it needs less GPU memory and moves less data per token. FP8 (weights and activations) roughly halves memory versus BF16 with very little quality loss on recent GPUs. Weight-only 4-bit methods such as AWQ and GPTQ cut memory about 4× and suit small-batch or single-GPU serving, with a larger quality drop, especially on small models. An FP8 KV cache frees memory for more concurrent sequences. The gains show up as fewer GPUs, higher throughput and lower cost per token, but quality must be measured on your own tasks, including Indian languages and long context. Compressing embedding vectors is a separate technique in module 5.
useCases: Fitting a 70B-class model on one or two GPUs
Cutting cost per token for self-hosted models
Running models on laptops and edge devices (GGUF)

items.detail: 8-bit weights and activations; Hopper-class GPUs and newer; usually within a fraction of a point
AWQ, GPTQ; about 0.5 byte per parameter plus overhead; bigger loss on small models
FP8 KV halves cache memory, so more sequences fit
a few hundred representative prompts to set scales
your own task scores, per language and context length, before and after

steps: Measure baseline quality, throughput and memory in BF16
Quantise with calibration data from your own traffic (FP8 first)
Serve with the quantised weights and, if needed, an FP8 KV cache
Re-run your evals per language and length; roll back if the loss exceeds your limit
pitfalls: Calibrating on English web text for a Hindi and Tamil workload
Judging quality on a general benchmark instead of your tasks
Assuming 4-bit is always faster; at large batch it can be slower than FP8
remember: Fewer bits, fewer GPUs; FP8 first, and measure on your own tasks.

practice.scenario: Nyaya Sahayak, a fictional legal-research service, self-hosts a 70B model so case files stay in its own cloud. In BF16 the model needs four 80 GB GPUs and costs about ₹208 per million tokens. It converts the weights to FP8, serves on two GPUs with an FP8 KV cache, and re-runs its Hindi and English legal Q&A evals: quality moves from 86.0 to 85.5 and cost falls to about ₹95 per million tokens. A 4-bit version would fit on one GPU but lose 1.5 points, so it is kept for a low-priority batch workload only.

library.what: Serves pre-quantised FP8, AWQ and GPTQ checkpoints and can store the KV cache in FP8.

practice.note: Needs GPUs that support FP8 (Hopper-class or newer) for the FP8 model; the model id is an example of a published FP8 checkpoint. Compare against the BF16 model on your own evals.

samples.code:
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

questions = [l.strip() for l in open("legal_qa_hi_en.txt", encoding="utf-8")][:200]
params = SamplingParams(max_tokens=256, temperature=0)

llm = LLM(model="RedHatAI/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-FP8-dynamic",
          tensor_parallel_size=2, kv_cache_dtype="fp8", max_model_len=8192)
outs = llm.generate(questions, params)

with open("answers_fp8.jsonl", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for q, o in zip(questions, outs):
        f.write(f'{{"q": {q!r}, "a": {o.outputs[0].text!r}}}\n')
print("wrote", len(outs), "answers; score them with the same grader as the BF16 run")

numericDrill.question: A 70B-parameter model in 4-bit weights uses 0.5 bytes per parameter plus 10% overhead for scales. How many GB of weights?
numericDrill.answer: 70 × 10⁹ × 0.5 = 35 GB; plus 10% = 38.5 GB, which fits on one 80 GB GPU with room for the KV cache.

interview.question: FP8 or INT4 for serving a 70B model?
interview.answer: FP8 first on GPUs that support it: half the memory with a very small quality change and good throughput at large batch. INT4 weight-only when you must fit on fewer GPUs or run small batches, after checking the larger quality loss on your tasks.

interview.question: What does KV-cache quantisation buy you?
interview.answer: The cache for each sequence takes half the memory in FP8, so more sequences fit at once and throughput rises, at a very small quality cost.
